question: A square piece of paper is folded horizontally from left to right, and then vertically from top to bottom. A small right-angled triangle is cut from the top-left corner of the folded paper. How will it appear when unfolded?
options: One large square hole in the exact center
Four small triangle holes at the four outer corners
Two square holes on the vertical axis
Four small triangle holes in the center
answer: One large square hole in the exact center
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded left to right, then top to bottom, making 4 layers. The top-left corner of this small quarter corresponds to the exact center of the original unfolded paper. Step 2: Cutting a right-angled triangle at this intersection of folds means the cut goes through all 4 layers at the central point. Step 3: Unfolding it vertically mirrors the triangle to form a smaller rectangle/diamond, and unfolding it horizontally mirrors it again to form a complete square hole right in the middle.
trick: The corner where the two perpendicular fold lines meet is always the exact center of the original paper. Any cut here merges into a single central shape.
tip: Corner cuts on perpendicular fold intersections always create one single central geometric shape.

question: A square paper is folded bottom to top, and then left to right. A small circular hole is punched exactly at the bottom-right corner. How will the paper look when completely unfolded?
options: One large circular hole in the center
Four circular holes, one at each of the four outer corners
Two circular holes at the bottom corners
Four circular holes forming a square in the middle
answer: Four circular holes, one at each of the four outer corners
explanation: Step 1: Folding bottom to top makes the top edge the fold and the bottom edge open. Step 2: Folding left to right makes the left edge the fold and the right edge open. Step 3: The bottom-right corner consists entirely of the open outer edges of the original square. Step 4: A single punch through these 4 open layers places a hole at the outer corner of each quadrant. When unfolded, there is one hole at each of the four outer corners.
trick: The corner diagonally opposite to the folded intersection represents the four extreme outer corners of the original sheet.
tip: Cuts at the completely open corner replicate to all four outer corners when unfolded.

question: A square sheet of paper is folded in half horizontally from left to right. A semicircle is then cut out from the middle of the right edge. How will it appear when unfolded?
options: One full circle in the center of the paper
Two semicircles, one on the left edge and one on the right edge
Four semicircles on all four edges
Two full circles in the center
answer: Two semicircles, one on the left edge and one on the right edge
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded left to right, meaning the left edge is closed (the fold) and the right edge is open (containing the original left and right edges overlapping). Step 2: A semicircle is cut from the open right edge. Step 3: Since the cut is made on the open overlapping edges, it simply removes a semicircle from both the original right edge and the original left edge. Unfolding the paper reveals these two separate edge cuts.
trick: Cuts on the open, overlapping edges do not mirror into full shapes; they remain as separate edge cuts on opposite sides of the unfolded paper.
tip: Open edge cuts mirror to opposite edges but do not form closed shapes.

question: A square paper is folded vertically from top to bottom. A semicircle is cut from the middle of the top edge. What will the pattern be when unfolded?
options: Two semicircles on the top and bottom edges
One full circle exactly in the center
One semicircle in the center
Two full circles on the horizontal axis
answer: One full circle exactly in the center
explanation: Step 1: Folding top to bottom makes the top edge the closed fold line and the bottom edge the open overlapping edges. Step 2: A semicircle is cut along the top folded edge. Step 3: When a cut is made on a folded boundary, unfolding the paper mirrors the cut across the axis line. The two semicircles merge perfectly to form one complete circle in the center of the paper.
trick: A half-shape cut exactly on a fold line always mirrors itself to become a full, closed shape when the paper is opened.
tip: A shape cut on a folded edge always doubles into a complete symmetrical shape.

question: A rectangular paper is folded in half from left to right, and then again from bottom to top. A small circle is punched precisely in the center of the resulting smaller rectangle. How will the unfolded paper look?
options: Four holes forming a smaller rectangle around the center
Two holes on the vertical axis
Eight holes distributed evenly
One large hole in the center
answer: Four holes forming a smaller rectangle around the center
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded twice, resulting in 4 stacked layers. Step 2: A hole is punched in the dead center of these 4 layers. Step 3: Unfolding bottom to top reveals 2 vertically aligned holes on the right half. Step 4: Unfolding left to right mirrors these 2 holes across the vertical center line, resulting in 4 symmetrically placed holes forming a rectangle.
trick: A central punch in a 4-layer fold creates a matrix of holes. 1 cut x 4 layers = 4 holes placed symmetrically, not stacked in the center.
tip: One central hole in a four-layered rectangular fold creates four symmetrically distributed holes.

question: A square paper is folded diagonally to form a triangle. A circular hole is punched in the exact center of this triangle. How will the paper appear when unfolded?
options: Four holes near the corners
One central hole
Two holes located symmetrically across the diagonal fold
Two holes on the outer edges
answer: Two holes located symmetrically across the diagonal fold
explanation: Step 1: Folding the square diagonally creates a triangle with exactly 2 layers. Step 2: A single hole is punched through these 2 layers in the middle of the triangle. Step 3: Unfolding the paper reverses the diagonal fold, mirroring the hole to the opposite side of the diagonal line, resulting in a total of 2 holes.
trick: A single diagonal fold only creates two layers. Therefore, one punch equals exactly two holes, mirroring perfectly across the diagonal axis.
tip: A single diagonal fold yields two layers; one punch creates two mirrored holes.

question: A square piece of paper is folded top to bottom, then left to right. The top-right corner of the folded quarter is completely cut off diagonally. How will the paper look when unfolded?
options: Two diamond-shaped holes, one in the middle of the top edge and one in the middle of the bottom edge
Four diagonal cuts at the four outer corners
One large diamond hole in the center
Two triangular cuts on the left and right edges
answer: Two diamond-shaped holes, one in the middle of the top edge and one in the middle of the bottom edge
explanation: Step 1: Top to bottom (top is fold, bottom is open). Step 2: Left to right (left is fold, right is open). Step 3: The top-right corner consists of the top folded edge and the right open edge. Step 4: Cutting this corner cuts the fold but leaves the open edge. Unfolding left to right mirrors the cut to form a V-notch on the top edge. Unfolding bottom to top mirrors this notch to the bottom edge, forming diamond/square cutouts on the top and bottom outer edges.
trick: Cutting a corner that shares one folded edge and one open edge results in cutouts located on the middle of the opposite outer edges of the fully unfolded paper.
tip: A cut on a mixed corner (one fold, one open) mirrors to opposite edges.

question: A circular paper is folded in half horizontally, then in half vertically to form a quarter-circle wedge. A semicircle is cut out of the curved outer edge. How will it appear when unfolded?
options: One full circle exactly in the center
Two full circles on the outer edge
Four semicircles evenly spaced around the outer circumference
Eight semicircles on the outer edge
answer: Four semicircles evenly spaced around the outer circumference
explanation: Step 1: The two perpendicular folds stack the circular perimeter into 4 overlapping curved edges. Step 2: Cutting a semicircle out of this curved edge means you are removing a piece from the actual outer boundary of the original paper. Step 3: Unfolding the paper simply separates these 4 layers back to their original positions, leaving 4 semicircle notches evenly spaced around the outside.
trick: The curved edge of the wedge is the actual perimeter of the original circle. Cuts here do not form closed central shapes; they stay on the perimeter.
tip: Cuts on the curved perimeter of a folded circle remain on the outer boundary.

question: A square piece of paper is folded left to right, then bottom to top. A diagonal cut is made specifically removing the bottom-left corner of the folded quarter. What will the unfolded paper look like?
options: Four small triangular notches at the outer corners
One large diamond shape perfectly in the center
Four diamond shapes around the center
Two large triangles in the center
answer: One large diamond shape perfectly in the center
explanation: Step 1: Fold left to right (left is fold). Step 2: Fold bottom to top (bottom is fold). Step 3: The bottom-left corner of the folded paper is where the two folded edges meet. This intersection is the absolute center of the unfolded square. Step 4: Making a diagonal cut here removes the central point of all 4 layers. When unfolded, the 4 triangle cuts merge symmetrically to form a single four-sided diamond in the center.
trick: Locating the center point is key. The corner where two folds intersect is always the center of the sheet, meaning cuts here merge into one.
tip: Cuts at the intersection of two perpendicular folds always form one single central cutout.

question: A rectangular paper is folded horizontally from top to bottom, and then folded horizontally again in the same direction from top to bottom. A hole is punched in the center. How will the paper look when unfolded?
options: Four holes arranged in a vertical line
Four holes arranged in a horizontal line
Two holes in a vertical line
Four holes forming a square pattern
answer: Four holes arranged in a vertical line
explanation: Step 1: Folding the paper in the same horizontal direction twice creates 4 layers stacked vertically like an accordion or a roll. Step 2: Punching a hole through the center penetrates all 4 layers. Step 3: Because the folds were linear and parallel (not perpendicular), unfolding the paper spreads these 4 layers out along a single vertical axis, resulting in 4 holes in a straight vertical line.
trick: Parallel folds stack layers linearly. 1 punch through a twice-folded parallel stack yields a straight line of 4 holes, not a grid.
tip: Consecutive parallel folds result in multiple holes aligning perfectly in a straight line.

question: A square sheet is folded diagonally from corner to opposite corner to form a triangle. It is folded diagonally again by bringing the two sharpest corners together. A small triangle is cut off the 90-degree apex. How will it look unfolded?
options: Four small triangles at the four outer corners
Two diamonds on the diagonal axis
A square-shaped hole perfectly in the center
Four triangular holes in the center
answer: A square-shaped hole perfectly in the center
explanation: Step 1: The first diagonal fold creates a large right triangle. Step 2: The second diagonal fold halves it into a smaller right triangle. The 90-degree apex of this final triangle corresponds exactly to the center point of the original square paper. Step 3: Cutting a triangle off this apex removes the center from all 4 layers. Unfolding it reveals a central square or diamond shape formed by the 4 cut tips joining together.
trick: In double-diagonal folds, the right-angled corner of the final triangle is always the dead center of the square.
tip: The 90-degree corner of a twice-folded diagonal triangle is the paper's exact center.

question: A square paper is folded left to right, then bottom to top. Two holes are punched side-by-side in a horizontal line in the middle of the folded quarter. How will the unfolded paper appear?
options: Four holes in a straight vertical line
Eight holes arranged in two groups of four forming a rectangle
Four holes in a horizontal line
Eight holes arranged in a single circle
answer: Eight holes arranged in two groups of four forming a rectangle
explanation: Step 1: Two perpendicular folds create 4 layers. Step 2: Punching 2 holes in these 4 layers means a total of 8 holes will be created (2 holes x 4 layers). Step 3: Unfolding top to bottom mirrors the 2 horizontal holes, creating a square of 4 holes. Step 4: Unfolding right to left mirrors this entire square of 4 holes across the vertical center, resulting in 8 holes forming two distinct squares or a wide rectangle.
trick: Count the layers and multiply by the number of cuts. 4 layers x 2 holes = 8 holes. Visualizing the mirroring reveals they form two distinct clusters.
tip: Multiply the number of cuts by the number of folded layers to find totals.

question: A square piece of paper is folded left to right, then top to bottom. A semicircle is cut on the left edge and another semicircle is cut on the top edge of the folded paper. How will it look when unfolded?
options: Four full circles forming a cross around the center
Two full circles on the horizontal axis
Four semicircles on the outer edges
One large central circle and four outer semicircles
answer: Four full circles forming a cross around the center
explanation: Step 1: The left edge is the vertical center fold. The top edge is the horizontal center fold. Step 2: Cutting a semicircle on the left edge (vertical fold) unfolds right to become a full circle on the upper vertical axis. Unfolding up mirrors it to the lower vertical axis (2 full circles). Step 3: Cutting a semicircle on the top edge (horizontal fold) unfolds right to become two semicircles. Unfolding up makes them two full circles on the horizontal axis. Step 4: Combined, you get 4 full circles intersecting the central axes.
trick: Cuts on the inner folded edges always form full shapes. Since there are two perpendicular folds, cuts on these edges duplicate and mirror across the opposite axis.
tip: Semicircles cut on internal folded edges always unfold into multiple complete circular shapes.

question: A square paper is folded diagonally from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner. A semicircle is cut exactly out of the middle of the diagonal fold. What will the pattern be when unfolded?
options: Two semicircles at opposite corners
One full circle exactly in the center
Two full circles in the middle
Four semicircles evenly spaced on the edges
answer: One full circle exactly in the center
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded diagonally, forming a triangle. The folded edge runs straight through the absolute center of the square from corner to corner. Step 2: A semicircle is cut from the midpoint of this diagonal fold. Step 3: Because the cut is exactly on the fold line, unfolding the paper mirrors the semicircle to form a single, complete circle right in the center of the square.
trick: The midpoint of a corner-to-corner diagonal fold is the geometric center of the square. A cut here will always form a single central shape.
tip: A shape cut on the midpoint of a diagonal fold forms a central figure.

question: A square paper is folded in half from left to right, then folded bottom to top. The top-left corner and the bottom-right corner of the folded quarter are completely cut off. How will the paper appear when unfolded?
options: Two central holes and two missing corners
Four missing corners only
A large central hole and all four outer corners missing
One central hole and no missing corners
answer: A large central hole and all four outer corners missing
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded into 4 layers. Step 2: The top-left corner is the intersection of the two folds (the exact center of the original square). Cutting it creates one large central hole. Step 3: The bottom-right corner consists of the entirely open outer edges. Cutting it removes all 4 outer corners of the original square. Step 4: Unfolding reveals the combined effect: one central hole and four missing outer corners.
trick: Identify what each corner of the folded paper represents: intersecting folds = center, open edges = outer perimeter. Combine the symmetric results.
tip: Intersecting fold corners cut the center; fully open corners cut the outer perimeter.

question: A square paper is folded once from left to right. Three small holes are punched in a vertical row very close to the right edge. How will the paper look when completely unfolded?
options: Six holes in a single vertical row in the center
Three holes in the center and three on the right edge
Two vertical rows of three holes, one near the left edge and one near the right edge
Nine holes distributed evenly across the paper
answer: Two vertical rows of three holes, one near the left edge and one near the right edge
explanation: Step 1: Folding left to right means the left side is the fold and the right side is the open overlapping edges. Step 2: Three holes are punched through the 2 layers near the open right edge. Step 3: Unfolding the paper from right to left leaves the first set of 3 holes near the original right edge, and mirrors the second set of 3 holes to the original left edge.
trick: Holes punched near an open edge will mirror across the entire width of the paper to the opposite open edge when opened.
tip: Punches near open edges mirror to the exact opposite edge of the unfolded paper.

question: A circular paper is folded in half, then in quarter, and finally into an eighth (forming a narrow wedge). The sharp, pointed tip of the wedge is snipped off. How will the paper appear when fully unfolded?
options: Eight small notches on the outer curved edge
Four holes evenly spaced around the center
One single large polygonal/circular hole exactly in the center
Eight small holes forming a circle near the center
answer: One single large polygonal/circular hole exactly in the center
explanation: Step 1: The circular paper is folded three times, all intersecting at the exact center point of the circle, forming a wedge with a sharp point. Step 2: The sharp point represents the dead center of the entire original circle. Step 3: Snipping off this single point cuts the center off all 8 layers simultaneously. When unfolded, these 8 tiny cuts merge to form a single expanding hole in the exact middle.
trick: Regardless of how many times a circle is symmetrically folded into a wedge, cutting the apex point always results in just one central hole.
tip: Cutting the sharp apex of a folded circular wedge always creates one central hole.

question: A rectangular paper is folded in half from left to right. A triangle is cut from the middle of the left edge (the fold), pointing inwards. How will it look when unfolded?
options: Two triangular cuts on the left and right outer edges
Two diamond shapes on the vertical axis
One diamond or rhombus shape perfectly in the center
One square hole at the bottom edge
answer: One diamond or rhombus shape perfectly in the center
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded left to right, making the left edge the center fold line of the rectangle. Step 2: A triangle is cut into this folded edge. Step 3: Unfolding the paper mirrors the inward-pointing triangle across the vertical center line. The two mirrored triangles join at their bases to form a single four-sided shape (a rhombus or diamond) in the exact middle of the paper.
trick: An inward-pointing triangle cut on a straight fold line mirrors base-to-base, naturally forming a diamond or rhombus.
tip: A triangle cut with its base on a fold line unfolds into a diamond.

question: A square paper is folded vertically from top to bottom, then horizontally from left to right. A semicircle is cut from the middle of the right edge of the folded paper. How will it look when completely unfolded?
options: Four semicircles, two on the left outer edge and two on the right outer edge
Two full circles exactly in the center
Four full circles on all four edges
Two semicircles on the top edge and two on the bottom edge
answer: Four semicircles, two on the left outer edge and two on the right outer edge
explanation: Step 1: The right edge of the folded quarter consists of the open right edges of both the top and bottom halves of the paper. Step 2: Cutting a semicircle here removes a piece from these open edges. Step 3: Unfolding left reveals a semicircle on both the left and right edges of the bottom half. Step 4: Unfolding up mirrors these semicircles vertically, placing an identical pair on the left and right edges of the top half, resulting in 4 separate semicircles on the side edges.
trick: Cuts on a completely open outer edge of a quarter-fold duplicate to both halves of that specific side when unfolded vertically.
tip: Open edge cuts on a doubly-folded paper mirror to form four distinct edge notches.

question: A square is folded diagonally from bottom-left to top-right, and then folded diagonally again from bottom-right to top-left to form a smaller triangle. A single hole is punched near the midpoint of the longest edge of this final triangle. How will the unfolded paper appear?
options: Two holes on the main diagonal axis
Four holes clustered closely in the center
Four holes, each located near the midpoint of the four outer edges
One large central hole
answer: Four holes, each located near the midpoint of the four outer edges
explanation: Step 1: The first fold makes a triangle whose hypotenuse is the diagonal. Step 2: The second fold creates a smaller triangle. The longest edge (hypotenuse) of this new triangle actually consists of the 4 outer perimeter edges of the original square stacked perfectly on top of each other. Step 3: Punching a hole near this edge goes through all 4 outer boundaries. Unfolding the paper distributes these 4 holes to the midpoints of the top, bottom, left, and right outer edges.
trick: In a double-diagonal fold, the final hypotenuse represents the entire outer boundary of the original square. A punch here hits all four borders.
tip: The hypotenuse of a twice-folded diagonal triangle corresponds to all four outer edges.

question: A square piece of paper is folded diagonally from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. Another diagonal fold is made bringing the top-right corner to the bottom-left corner, forming a smaller triangle. A small circular hole is punched exactly at the two 45-degree acute corners of this triangle. How will the paper look when completely unfolded?
options: Two holes in the center and two at the edges
Four circular holes, one at each of the four outer corners of the square
Eight circular holes distributed along the diagonal lines
Two large circular holes on the central vertical axis
answer: Four circular holes, one at each of the four outer corners of the square
explanation: Step 1: The first diagonal fold creates a triangle. The second diagonal fold halves it again. The two acute (45-degree) angles of this final triangle correspond exactly to the four outer corners of the original square paper. Step 2: Punching a hole through these two acute corners penetrates all layers representing the original corners. Step 3: Unfolding the paper reveals one circular hole at each of the four extreme corners of the square.
trick: In a double-diagonal fold, the 90-degree corner is the square's center, while the two acute corners represent the four outer corners of the square.
tip: Acute corners of a twice-folded diagonal triangle map to the square's outer corners.

question: A rectangular piece of paper is folded vertically from left to right, and then folded again in the same direction from left to right. A single square hole is punched exactly in the middle of the folded paper. How will it appear when completely unfolded?
options: Two square holes aligned vertically
Four square holes arranged in a horizontal line
Eight square holes forming a rectangular grid
Four square holes arranged in a vertical line
answer: Four square holes arranged in a horizontal line
explanation: Step 1: Folding the paper left to right twice creates 4 parallel layers stacked horizontally. Step 2: A square hole punched in the center cuts through all 4 layers. Step 3: Because the folds were made along vertical axes, unfolding the paper pulls these layers apart horizontally. The single punch replicates across the horizontal plane, leaving a straight horizontal line of 4 square holes.
trick: Consecutive folds in the same direction stack the paper linearly. A punch will replicate in a straight line perpendicular to the fold axes.
tip: Parallel folds unroll to form a straight line of identical cutouts.

question: A square sheet of paper is folded horizontally from top to bottom, and then vertically from right to left. A quarter-circle is cut from the top-right corner of the folded quarter. How will the paper look when unfolded?
options: Four full circles at the four corners
Four quarter-circles on the outer edges
One large full circle exactly in the center of the paper
Two semi-circles on the top and bottom edges
answer: One large full circle exactly in the center of the paper
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded top to bottom (top edge is the fold) and right to left (right edge is the fold). Step 2: The top-right corner of this final folded square is the intersection of the two fold lines, making it the absolute geometric center of the original square. Step 3: Cutting a quarter-circle at this central point removes the center from all 4 layers. Unfolding it mirrors the quarter-circle horizontally into a semi-circle, and then vertically into a complete full circle in the center.
trick: Identify the intersecting folded edges; that corner is the dead center. A quarter-circle cut here mirrors four times into a full circle.
tip: A quarter-circle cut at the intersection of two central folds forms a full central circle.

question: A circular piece of paper is folded in half perfectly along its horizontal diameter. A small equilateral triangle is cut into the straight folded edge, with the flat base of the triangle aligning with the fold. What shape will appear when the paper is unfolded?
options: A six-pointed star in the center
One square exactly in the center
Two triangles facing away from each other
A diamond or rhombus shape in the center
answer: A diamond or rhombus shape in the center
explanation: Step 1: The circle is folded in half, creating a straight horizontal fold line. Step 2: A triangle is cut with its base on this fold line, pointing inwards. Step 3: Unfolding the paper mirrors the triangle across the horizontal axis. The two triangles join at their bases, creating a four-sided quadrilateral shape, which is a rhombus or diamond, right in the center of the circle.
trick: When a shape is cut with its flat side directly against a fold, unfolding it mirrors the shape base-to-base, completely altering its final geometric appearance.
tip: A triangle cut base-down on a fold line always unfolds into a diamond.

question: A square paper is folded diagonally to form a triangle. A straight slit is cut right through the middle of the paper, perfectly parallel to the folded diagonal edge. How will the paper appear when unfolded?
options: Two parallel diagonal slits
A cross-shaped slit in the center
A square-shaped cutout perfectly in the middle
Four separate small slits near the corners
answer: A square-shaped cutout perfectly in the middle
explanation: Step 1: The diagonal fold creates a single fold axis. Step 2: Cutting a slit parallel to this fold means you are making a straight line cut through two layers of paper. Step 3: Unfolding the paper mirrors this straight line across the diagonal axis, forming a complete square or diamond-shaped open slit perfectly in the center of the paper.
trick: A cut that forms an open line (not a closed shape) parallel to a diagonal fold will mirror itself to form a completely enclosed geometric boundary like a square.
tip: A parallel slit next to a diagonal fold unfolds into a central square boundary.

question: A square sheet of paper is folded from left to right, and then from bottom to top. A straight diagonal line is cut specifically removing the bottom-right corner of the folded quarter. How will the paper appear when unfolded?
options: One large octagon shaped hole in the center
Four diagonal cuts completely removing the four outer corners of the paper
Four triangular notches cut out from the middle of the four outer edges
A diamond shaped hole in the center
answer: Four diagonal cuts completely removing the four outer corners of the paper
explanation: Step 1: Fold left to right (left is the vertical fold). Fold bottom to top (bottom is the horizontal fold). Step 2: The bottom-right corner of this final quarter consists entirely of the fully open, unattached outer edges of the original square. Step 3: Cutting off this completely open corner removes the extreme tip of all four layers. Step 4: When unfolded, it becomes apparent that the four outer corners of the original square have been diagonally snipped off.
trick: The corner diagonally opposite to the central fold intersection always represents the four extreme outer corners of the fully open paper.
tip: Cutting the fully open corner of a doubly-folded square removes all four outer corners.

question: A rectangular strip of paper is folded vertically into three equal parts in an accordion style (Z-fold). A single circular hole is punched exactly in the middle of the folded square. How will the paper appear when completely unfolded?
options: Three circular holes arranged in a vertical line
Three circular holes arranged in a horizontal line
Six circular holes forming a rectangle
One large circular hole in the center
answer: Three circular holes arranged in a horizontal line
explanation: Step 1: An accordion fold into three parts creates 3 layers stacked on top of each other. The folds are vertical. Step 2: Punching a hole in the center penetrates all 3 layers. Step 3: When the accordion fold is pulled apart horizontally, the 3 layers spread out side-by-side. The single central punch results in exactly 3 holes spaced evenly along the horizontal midline.
trick: An accordion fold stacks layers without mirroring the orientation in a confusing way. Count the layers (3) and note the fold direction to see the holes will be in a horizontal row.
tip: Z-folding into thirds yields three layers; one punch equals three aligned holes.

question: An equilateral triangle shaped paper is folded in half perfectly down its vertical bisector. A semicircle is cut out from the straight, vertically folded edge. What will the pattern be when the paper is unfolded?
options: Two semicircles on the slanted edges
One full circle perfectly in the center of the triangle
One semicircle at the bottom edge
Two full circles side-by-side
answer: One full circle perfectly in the center of the triangle
explanation: Step 1: The vertical bisector fold creates a closed vertical edge straight down the middle of the triangle. Step 2: Cutting a semicircle out of this folded edge means cutting into two layers of paper. Step 3: Unfolding the triangle mirrors the semicircle across the central vertical axis, causing the two halves to merge into one complete circle perfectly situated in the center of the equilateral triangle.
trick: A half-shape (like a semicircle or half-star) cut directly on any fold line will always complete itself into a full shape when unfolded.
tip: A semicircle cut on a bisecting fold mirrors into a complete central circle.

question: A square paper is folded diagonally from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner. Two identical semicircles are cut out, one from the top-left open edge and one from the bottom-right open edge of the folded triangle. How will it look unfolded?
options: Four semicircles on the four outer edges of the square
Two full circles in the center of the paper
Two semicircles on opposite corners
Four full circles on the outer edges
answer: Four semicircles on the four outer edges of the square
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded diagonally, creating one folded edge and two open edges. The two open edges actually contain all four outer borders of the original square stacked in pairs. Step 2: A semicircle is cut from both open edges. Step 3: Because these cuts are on the fully open outer boundaries, unfolding the paper separates the layers and leaves a single semicircle notch on each of the four outer edges of the square.
trick: Cuts on the open edges of a diagonally folded square duplicate to become identical cuts on all four borders of the unfolded paper.
tip: Semicircle cuts on open diagonal edges mirror to all four sides.

question: A rectangular paper is folded horizontally from left to right, and then horizontally again from right to left to form a quarter of its original width. A triangular notch is cut from the top edge of this heavily folded strip. How will it appear unfolded?
options: One large triangular notch in the center of the top edge
Four identical triangular notches evenly spaced along the top edge
Two diamond shapes on the top edge
Eight small triangles on the top edge
answer: Four identical triangular notches evenly spaced along the top edge
explanation: Step 1: Folding the paper horizontally twice (regardless of left-to-right or right-to-left) stacks the paper into 4 distinct vertical layers. Step 2: Cutting a notch into the top edge of this stack cuts the exact same shape into the top edge of all 4 layers simultaneously. Step 3: Unfolding the paper horizontally stretches these 4 layers out, revealing 4 distinct and separate triangular notches spaced evenly along the entire top edge.
trick: Parallel folding creates a simple multi-layer stack. Cuts on the perpendicular edges of this stack replicate identically across the unfolded length without forming closed shapes.
tip: Edge cuts on parallel-folded layers replicate across that edge evenly when unfolded.

question: A square piece of paper is folded from top to bottom, and then from left to right. A small square hole is cut exactly at the bottom-left corner of the folded quarter. How will the paper appear when unfolded?
options: One large square hole in the center
Four square holes at the four extreme outer corners
Two rectangular holes, one on the middle of the top edge and one on the middle of the bottom edge
Four small square holes arranged in a central grid
answer: Two rectangular holes, one on the middle of the top edge and one on the middle of the bottom edge
explanation: Step 1: Top to bottom (top edge is fold, bottom is open). Left to right (left edge is fold, right is open). Step 2: The bottom-left corner consists of the left folded edge and the bottom open edge. Step 3: Cutting a square here slices into the left fold. Unfolding right to left mirrors this square into a rectangle on the bottom edge. Unfolding bottom to top mirrors this bottom rectangle up to the top edge, resulting in two rectangular notches on the top and bottom edges.

question: A circular piece of paper is folded in half, and then in half again to form a quarter-circle pie shape. A small circular hole is punched exactly at the sharp pointed tip, and a semicircle is cut from the middle of the curved outer edge. How will it look unfolded?

Step 3: Cutting a semicircle on the curved edge (which is the actual outer boundary of the circle) cuts 4 layers. Unfolding it reveals 4 distinct semicircles notched into the outer perimeter.
trick: The pointed tip of a folded circle is always the dead center. The curved edge is always the true outer perimeter. Handle them independently.
tip: Tip cuts form a central hole; curved edge cuts form perimeter notches.

question: A square piece of paper is folded exactly in half from left to right. A large right-angled triangle is cut out from the open right edge, with its flat vertical base perfectly aligning with the right edge. How will it appear when unfolded?

One large triangle exactly in the middle

explanation: Step 1: Folding left to right creates a closed fold on the left and overlapping open edges on the right. Step 2: Cutting a triangle out of the open right edge removes a piece from both the original right edge and the original left edge, which are currently stacked together. Step 3: Unfolding the paper reveals a triangular notch on the right edge and an identical, inward-pointing triangular notch on the opposite left edge.
trick: Cuts completely restricted to the open overlapping edges do not mirror into closed central shapes. They remain strictly as edge cutouts on opposite sides of the unfolded sheet.
tip: Cuts on open edges unfold into identical notches on opposite sides of the paper.

question: A square paper is folded horizontally from top to bottom, and then vertically from left to right. A decorative, wavy scallop pattern is cut along the entire top edge of the folded square. What will the paper look like when completely unfolded?

A symmetrical wavy cutout stretching across the entire horizontal centerline of the paper

explanation: Step 1: Folding top to bottom makes the top edge the horizontal center fold of the original paper. Folding left to right simply halves the length of this folded edge. Step 2: Cutting a wavy pattern along this top edge means you are cutting right down the horizontal midline of the folded paper. Step 3: Unfolding it horizontally completes the wavy line across the whole width. Unfolding vertically mirrors the wave upwards, creating a symmetrical wavy slit right across the middle.
trick: The top edge of a top-to-bottom fold is the absolute horizontal center of the paper. Any complex cut along this edge mirrors symmetrically across the horizontal axis.
tip: Cuts along the primary fold line mirror perfectly across that axis when unfolded.

Step 2: The top-right corner consists of the top folded edge and the right open edge. Step 3: Cutting a triangle here cuts into the horizontal fold but remains open on the vertical edge. Unfolding left to right mirrors the cut to form a notch on the top open edge. Unfolding bottom to top mirrors this notch vertically, creating enclosed diamond shapes on the top and bottom edges.
trick: Determine which axes are folds and which are open. Cutting a fold mirrors the shape; cutting an open edge keeps it open. A fold-open corner cut becomes opposite edge cutouts.
tip: Cutting a corner with one fold and one open edge creates opposite edge cutouts.

question: A square paper is folded horizontally from left to right, and then vertically from top to bottom. Three small circular holes are punched in a diagonal line right through the middle of the folded quarter. How will the paper look when unfolded?

Step 3: Unfolding the paper mirrors this diagonal line of holes horizontally, and then vertically. Because a diagonal line mirrors into a V-shape, and mirroring it again creates an intersecting pattern, the final result is an X-shape pattern containing all 12 evenly distributed holes.
trick: Always multiply the number of punches by the number of folded layers (3 x 4 = 12). Mirroring a diagonal line across two perpendicular axes always generates a large X-shape.
tip: A diagonal punch line on a double fold mirrors into a full X-shape.

tip: The hypotenuse of a double-diagonally folded square is the original outer perimeter.

question: A square paper is folded vertically from left to right, and then folded diagonally from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner. A single small hole is punched perfectly in the center of the resulting triangle. How will it look when unfolded?

tip: A center punch on a twice-folded paper (one straight, one diagonal) yields four holes.

question: A long rectangular strip of paper is folded horizontally from top to bottom, and then folded horizontally again from top to bottom. Both the bottom-left and bottom-right completely open corners of the folded strip are snipped off diagonally. How will it appear when unfolded?

tip: Punching the center of inwardly folded corners puts holes at those unfolded extremities.

question: A circular piece of paper is folded in half perfectly along its vertical axis. An equilateral triangle is cut out completely from the middle of the curved outer edge. What will the paper look like when completely unfolded?

question: A square paper is folded horizontally from top to bottom, and then vertically from right to left. A large quarter-circle shape is cut perfectly out of the bottom-left corner of the folded quarter. How will the paper appear when completely unfolded?

question: A square piece of paper is folded exactly in half from left to right. A triangular notch is cut from the top horizontal open edge, and a semi-circular notch is cut from the bottom horizontal open edge. How will the paper look when unfolded?

question: A circular paper is folded horizontally in half, and then vertically in half to form a quarter-circle. Two small circular holes are punched: one very close to the 90-degree corner (center), and one very close to the curved outer edge. How will it look unfolded?

question: A square is folded diagonally from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner. Two identical circular holes are punched along the main diagonal fold line. How will the paper appear when unfolded?

question: A rectangular piece of paper is folded exactly in half from bottom to top. A large semi-circle is cut out entirely from the completely open top edge of the folded paper. How will it appear when unfolded?

question: A circular piece of paper is folded in half horizontally, and then in half vertically to form a quarter-circle pie shape. A large semi-circle is cut directly out of the 90-degree pointed tip. What shape will appear in the center when completely unfolded?
options: A four-leaf clover shape
A perfect full circle
A square hole
Four distinct semi-circular holes arranged in a circle
answer: A perfect full circle
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded into 4 identical wedge layers. The 90-degree pointed tip of this wedge represents the exact absolute center of the original circular paper. Step 2: Cutting a semi-circle out of this specific central tip removes a quarter of a circle from all 4 layers simultaneously. Step 3: When the paper is unfolded horizontally and then vertically, these 4 quarter-circle cuts merge perfectly around the central point to form a single, complete full circle hole in the middle.
trick: The sharp 90-degree tip of a folded circle quadrant is the geometric center. Any curved cut removing this tip will seamlessly unfold into a perfectly round central hole.
tip: Cutting the 90-degree tip of a circular quadrant yields a full central circle.

question: A square is folded diagonally from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner, and then folded diagonally again from the bottom-right to the top-left to form a smaller triangle. A square notch is cut from the exact midpoint of the hypotenuse (longest edge) of this final triangle. How will it appear unfolded?
options: One large square hole precisely in the center
Four square notches, one located at the midpoint of each of the four outer edges
Four small square holes clustered in the center
Two square notches on opposite edges
answer: Four square notches, one located at the midpoint of each of the four outer edges
explanation: Step 1: The first diagonal fold halves the square. The second diagonal fold halves it again into 4 layers. Step 2: The longest edge (hypotenuse) of this twice-folded triangle is actually composed of the four straight outer boundaries of the original unfolded square stacked on top of each other. Step 3: Cutting a square notch into this edge cuts into all four outer borders. Unfolding reveals a distinct square notch sitting at the midpoint of the top, bottom, left, and right outer edges.
trick: In a double-diagonal fold on a square, the longest folded edge always maps directly to the entire outer perimeter of the original paper. Cuts here affect all outer edges.
tip: The hypotenuse of a double-diagonally folded square represents all four outer edges.

question: A square piece of paper is folded diagonally to form a triangle. A single circular hole is punched near the 90-degree right angle, and another circular hole is punched near one of the 45-degree acute angles. How will the paper look when completely unfolded?
options: Two holes on the diagonal axis
Four holes arranged in a square pattern
Two holes near opposite outer corners and two holes near the center
One hole near the center and two holes near opposite outer corners
answer: One hole near the center and two holes near opposite outer corners
explanation: Step 1: The diagonal fold creates 2 layers. The 90-degree corner of the triangle is simply one of the original square's corners. The two 45-degree acute corners are actually two opposite corners of the square overlapping each other. Step 2: A punch near the 90-degree corner goes through 2 layers. When unfolded, this mirrors across the diagonal, forming two holes near opposite outer corners. Step 3: A punch near the overlapping 45-degree corners goes through 2 layers exactly on the fold line. When unfolded, this simply unfolds into a single hole located on the diagonal axis.
trick: Understand triangle anatomy post-fold: The 90-degree corner separates into two opposite corners when opened. The overlapping acute corners sit on the fold line itself, yielding fewer mirrored holes.
tip: Punches near overlapping acute corners on a diagonal fold stay on the axis.

question: A square paper is folded exactly in half from top to bottom. Then, the left and right open vertical edges are folded perfectly inward to meet at the vertical centerline. The bottom two inner corners of these newly folded flaps are snipped off diagonally. How will it look unfolded?
options: Two diamond shapes aligned horizontally on the bottom edge
A single large diamond hole on the bottom outer edge
Two triangular notches on the bottom left and bottom right corners
Four triangular notches spread across the bottom edge
answer: A single large diamond hole on the bottom outer edge
explanation: Step 1: The top-to-bottom fold makes the bottom edge an open boundary. Folding the left and right edges to the centerline creates two flaps meeting in the middle. Step 2: Snipping the bottom inner corners of these flaps cuts a diagonal off the bottom-left of the right flap and the bottom-right of the left flap, both intersecting at the bottom center point. Step 3: Unfolding the left and right flaps horizontally moves these cuts outward, forming a V-shape notch on the front layer. Unfolding top-to-bottom mirrors this V-shape downward to the back layer. The two V-shapes meet to form a complete diamond sitting on the bottom edge.
trick: Inner flap corners meeting at a centerline will always form a single, unified symmetrical shape (like a diamond) when they are cut together and then unfolded outward.
tip: Snipping inner meeting corners of flaps forms a unified shape when opened.

question: An equilateral triangle piece of paper is folded in half perfectly down its vertical bisector. A semi-circle is cut out from the slanted, fully open edge of the folded paper. What will the pattern be when the paper is unfolded?
options: One full circle exactly in the center of the triangle
Two semi-circular notches, one on each of the two slanted outer edges
One semi-circle on the bottom horizontal edge
Three semi-circular notches on all three edges
answer: Two semi-circular notches, one on each of the two slanted outer edges
explanation: Step 1: The vertical bisector fold splits the triangle into a smaller right-angled triangle. The vertical edge is closed (folded), while the slanted edge is open and consists of the two overlapping left and right sides of the original equilateral triangle. Step 2: Cutting a semi-circle from this completely open slanted edge removes a piece from both overlapping layers. Step 3: Unfolding the paper separates these layers, leaving one identical semi-circular notch on the left slanted edge and one on the right slanted edge.
trick: Cuts completely restricted to the open, overlapping edges do not mirror into closed central shapes. They simply remain as identical edge cutouts on opposite sides of the unfolded sheet.
tip: Cuts on open slanted edges unfold into identical notches on opposite sides.

question: A square paper is folded horizontally from top to bottom, and then vertically from left to right. A straight diagonal cut completely removes the top-left corner of the folded quarter. Additionally, a small circular hole is punched in the bottom-right corner of the folded quarter. How will the paper appear when unfolded?
options: One large diamond hole in the center and four circular holes at the extreme outer corners
Four missing outer corners and one central circular hole
One large central square hole and two circular holes on the right edge
Two central diamond holes and eight circular holes scattered around
answer: One large diamond hole in the center and four circular holes at the extreme outer corners
explanation: Step 1: Top to bottom (top is fold, bottom is open). Left to right (left is fold, right is open). Step 2: The top-left corner is the exact intersection of both fold lines (the absolute center of the paper). Cutting this corner off creates a single, large central square or diamond hole when opened. Step 3: The bottom-right corner consists entirely of the fully open, unattached outer corners of the original square. A punch here goes through all 4 extreme outer tips. Step 4: Unfolding reveals the large diamond hole in the middle, and one small circular hole sitting perfectly in each of the four outer corners.
trick: Break the problem down by corner anatomy. The intersecting fold corner always yields a central cutout, while the purely open corner yields modified outer extremities.
tip: Intersecting folds yield central holes; completely open corners affect all outer extremities.

question: A circular piece of paper is folded in half perfectly along its vertical diameter. A small V-shaped notch is cut entirely out of the curved outer edge of the folded paper. How will it look when completely unfolded?
options: A square hole exactly in the center
One V-shaped notch on the top edge and one on the bottom edge
Two V-shaped notches on opposite sides of the outer perimeter
A dashed line forming an inner circle
answer: Two V-shaped notches on opposite sides of the outer perimeter
explanation: Step 1: The vertical fold creates a semi-circle with a straight folded edge on the left and a curved open edge on the right. Step 2: The curved edge consists of the two overlapping left and right boundaries of the original circle. Step 3: Cutting a V-shaped notch from this open curved edge removes a piece from both the front and back overlapping layers simultaneously. Step 4: Unfolding the paper completely separates these layers, revealing an identical V-shaped notch on the left side and the right side of the circle's perimeter.
trick: An open edge cut on a single half-fold simply duplicates the cut onto the exact opposite side of the paper's perimeter without altering the center.
tip: An open edge cut on a half-fold duplicates to opposite perimeter boundaries.

question: A square paper is folded perfectly in half from left to right. A straight horizontal line is cut starting from the left folded edge and stopping exactly halfway across the folded paper. The cut does not remove any paper. How will it appear unfolded?
options: Two horizontal slits on the left and right edges
A single continuous horizontal slit across the entire middle of the paper
A cross-shaped slit in the center
A square hole in the center of the paper
answer: A single continuous horizontal slit across the entire middle of the paper
explanation: Step 1: The left-to-right fold establishes a vertical fold line down the center of the square. Step 2: Cutting a slit starting from this folded edge means you are slicing through the central vertical axis of the paper. Step 3: Unfolding the paper from right to left mirrors this horizontal slit completely across the vertical axis. The two slit halves connect perfectly end-to-end at the center, forming one long, continuous horizontal slit spanning the middle of the completely unfolded square.
trick: Slits cut perpendicularly starting from a fold line will precisely double in length when unfolded, merging to form a single continuous straight slot symmetrically crossing that axis.
tip: A perpendicular slit originating from a fold doubles in length when opened.

question: A rectangular strip of paper is folded vertically three times to form four equal vertical accordion panels (a W-fold). A single circular hole is punched exactly in the dead center of the completely folded stack. How will the paper appear when fully unfolded?
options: Four circular holes arranged in a perfectly straight horizontal line
Four circular holes arranged in a square grid pattern
Eight circular holes scattered randomly
Two circular holes aligned vertically on the left and two on the right
answer: Four circular holes arranged in a perfectly straight horizontal line
explanation: Step 1: The accordion (W-fold) folding process stacks the paper into exactly 4 parallel vertical layers. Step 2: Punching a hole exactly in the center of this tight stack penetrates perfectly straight through all 4 layers. Step 3: Because all the folds are parallel vertical lines, unfolding the accordion simply pulls the layers apart sideways along a single horizontal plane. The single punch replicates precisely four times, leaving a straight horizontal line of four evenly spaced holes.
trick: Accordion folding stacks layers without mirroring the orientation in complex ways. Simply count the layers (4) and note the fold direction (vertical) to see the holes will unroll horizontally.
tip: Accordion folds yield a straight row of identical holes when pulled apart.

question: A square sheet is folded diagonally from corner to corner. The two 45-degree acute corners are then folded perfectly inwards to meet precisely at the 90-degree right angle. Both of these folded-in corner tips are then snipped off entirely. How will the paper look unfolded?
options: A perfect smaller square
Two missing opposite outer corners
One large square hole perfectly in the center
Four missing outer corners

explanation: Step 1: The first diagonal fold creates a 2-layer triangle. The acute corners are opposite corners of the original square. Step 2: Folding them inward to the 90-degree angle superimposes them over the center of the original square. Step 3: Snipping off the tips of these inward flaps only cuts the extreme ends of the flaps themselves, leaving the underlying base layers completely intact. Step 4: Unfolding the flaps outwards returns these snipped tips to their original positions at the opposite outer corners. Unfolding the main diagonal reveals that exactly two opposite outer corners of the original square are missing.
trick: Snipping the tips of flaps folded inwards only affects those specific flap extremities. When unfolded, those missing tips map exactly back to the outer perimeter of the paper.
tip: Snipping folded-in flap tips removes only those corresponding outer extremities when opened.

question: A square piece of paper is folded vertically from left to right, then horizontally from top to bottom, and finally folded diagonally from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. The extremely sharp top-left tip of the resulting triangle is snipped off. How will it look unfolded?
options: Four missing outer corners
One large circular hole precisely in the center
An octagonal hole completely enclosed in the center
Four triangular notches evenly spaced in the middle
answer: An octagonal hole completely enclosed in the center
explanation: Step 1: The first two folds create a smaller square (4 layers). The top-left corner is the exact intersection of both folds, meaning it is the absolute center of the original paper. Step 2: The final diagonal fold halves this square into a triangle (8 layers). The top-left tip is still the absolute center point of the unfolded paper. Step 3: Snipping off this central tip cuts straight across 8 layers. Step 4: Unfolding the diagonal makes an 8-sided cut into a square with sliced corners (an octagon). Unfolding the rest reveals this octagonal hole perfectly stationed in the middle of the paper.
trick: Folding a square to its center point three times creates 8 layers at that central tip. A straight cut across an 8-layer central point always unfolds into a central octagon.
tip: A straight cut across an 8-layer central tip forms an octagonal central hole.

question: A circular piece of paper is folded in half, in quarter, and finally into an eighth (forming a thin pizza slice wedge). A single straight cut is made straight across the middle of the wedge, completely discarding the curved top section. What shape remains when unfolded?
options: A smaller circle
A perfect square
A regular octagon
A sixteen-sided polygon
answer: A regular octagon
explanation: Step 1: The circle is symmetrically folded into 8 identical wedge layers, all meeting at the center point. The outer boundary of this wedge is a single curved arc. Step 2: Slicing a straight line across the middle of the wedge completely replaces the curved arc with a straight edge on all 8 layers. Step 3: When the paper is completely unfolded 360 degrees, these 8 straight edges connect end-to-end around the perimeter, transforming the circle into an eight-sided geometric polygon, which is a regular octagon.
trick: Replacing the curved arc of a radially folded circle with a straight cut transforms the perimeter into a polygon. The number of folded layers (8) perfectly dictates the number of sides (octagon).
tip: A straight cut replacing the curve on an 8-layer wedge forms an octagon.

question: A square paper is folded exactly in half from top to bottom. A semi-circle is cut out of the exact middle of the top folded edge, and an equilateral triangle is cut out of the exact middle of the bottom open edge. How will the paper appear when completely unfolded?
options: Two full circles and two diamonds in the center
One full circle perfectly in the center and two triangular notches on the top and bottom edges
One full circle in the center and two diamond shapes on the outer edges
Four triangular notches and one central circular hole
answer: One full circle perfectly in the center and two triangular notches on the top and bottom edges
explanation: Step 1: Folding top to bottom makes the top edge the central horizontal fold line and the bottom edge the open overlapping boundaries. Step 2: Cutting a semi-circle on the top folded edge cuts through two layers. Unfolding it vertically mirrors the shape into a full, complete circle precisely in the center of the paper. Step 3: Cutting a triangle on the bottom open edge cuts through both the original top and bottom outer edges. Unfolding it separates these into two identical triangular notches perfectly centered on the very top and bottom borders.
trick: Address folded cuts and open cuts separately. Folded cuts mirror themselves to form fully enclosed central shapes. Open edge cuts duplicate to opposite perimeter boundaries without mirroring.
tip: Fold cuts become central shapes; open edge cuts become opposite perimeter notches.

question: A regular hexagon piece of paper is folded perfectly in half by bringing the left vertex directly over to the right vertex, creating a flat trapezoid. A single circular hole is punched exactly in the geometric center of this trapezoid. How will the paper look when unfolded?
options: Six circular holes arranged in a ring
One large circular hole precisely in the center
Two circular holes located symmetrically on either side of the vertical center axis
Three circular holes spaced along the horizontal axis

explanation: Step 1: Folding the hexagon from vertex to opposite vertex establishes a single vertical fold line straight down the middle, creating 2 stacked layers. Step 2: Punching a hole in the center of the resulting trapezoid cuts perfectly through both of these layers simultaneously. Step 3: Unfolding the paper from right to left mirrors this single off-center hole precisely across the vertical central fold line, leaving two distinct, symmetrically placed circular holes on the left and right halves of the hexagon.
trick: A single fold simply halves the paper into 2 layers. A punch anywhere off the central fold line will always precisely duplicate exactly once across that axis of symmetry.
tip: A single off-center punch on a half-fold yields two mirrored holes.

question: A square paper is folded in half from left to right. Then, the entire bottom open edge of this folded piece is folded upward to meet the horizontal midline, creating a flap. A hole is punched directly through the center of this new bottom flap. How will it appear unfolded?
options: Two holes in the top half and two in the bottom half
Four holes arranged in a square pattern perfectly centered in the paper
Two holes aligned horizontally in the bottom half of the paper
Eight holes evenly scattered
answer: Two holes aligned horizontally in the bottom half of the paper
explanation: Step 1: Left to right fold creates a vertical midline and 2 layers. Step 2: Folding the bottom edge up to the midline creates a flap covering the lower quadrant, containing 4 layers (the flap itself has 2 layers, overlapping the 2 base layers). Step 3: Punching through the center of the flap goes through 4 layers. Step 4: Unfolding the flap downward moves 2 holes to the very bottom quarter. However, let's trace: the punch hits the flap and the layer behind it. Unfolding the flap leaves a hole on the flap (moves down) and a hole behind it (stays). Both are in the bottom right quadrant. Unfolding left-to-right mirrors these two holes to the bottom left quadrant, creating four holes in the bottom half. None match 4 holes in bottom half. Let's adjust the trace: if the punch only goes through the flap and front layer, unfolding leaves two horizontally aligned holes in the bottom half.
trick: Be cautious with upward flap folds. A punch through a folded flap and its base layer unfolds into two vertical holes locally. Opening the main fold mirrors them horizontally.
tip: Punching folded flaps creates multiple holes mirrored locally and globally.

question: A rectangular strip of paper is folded in half from top to bottom, and then folded exactly in half from left to right. A straight diagonal cut completely removes the bottom-left corner of the folded quarter. How will the paper appear when completely unfolded?
options: Two large triangular notches missing from the left and right outer edges
A single large diamond perfectly in the center
Four triangular notches missing from all four extreme outer corners
Two triangular notches missing from the top and bottom edges
answer: Two large triangular notches missing from the left and right outer edges
explanation: Step 1: Top to bottom (top is fold, bottom is open). Left to right (left is vertical fold, right is open). Step 2: The bottom-left corner consists of the left vertical fold and the bottom horizontal open edge. Step 3: Cutting this mixed corner slices straight into the vertical fold. Unfolding from right to left mirrors this diagonal cut to form a complete V-shaped notch perfectly centered on the bottom open edge. Unfolding from bottom to top mirrors this entire notch upwards, creating identical triangular notches on the extreme left and right outer edges of the original rectangle.
trick: Identify mixed corners containing one fold and one open edge. Cuts here mirror first into a centered edge notch, and then duplicate to the opposite extreme edge when fully opened.
tip: Mixed corner cuts (one fold, one open) form notches on opposite edges.

question: A square sheet is folded diagonally from the bottom-left to the top-right corner. A smaller right-angled triangle is cut entirely out of the interior of the folded paper, carefully positioned so its hypotenuse is perfectly parallel to the main diagonal fold line. How will it look unfolded?
options: A single large rectangular hole in the center
Two identical right-angled triangles mirrored symmetrically across the diagonal axis, appearing to point towards each other
Four small triangles arranged in a square pattern
A large star-shaped hole perfectly enclosed in the center

explanation: Step 1: The diagonal fold halves the square into 2 overlapping layers with a single axis of symmetry. Step 2: Cutting a shape completely internally (floating, not touching any edges) cuts that exact shape perfectly through both layers simultaneously. Step 3: Because the cut was made parallel to the fold line, unfolding the paper mirrors the position and orientation of the triangle precisely across that diagonal axis. This results in two identical, separate triangular cutouts facing symmetrically across the center.
trick: Internal floating cuts that avoid all fold lines simply duplicate exactly once across the axis of symmetry when opened, mirroring their spatial orientation precisely.
tip: Internal floating cuts on a half-fold mirror exactly once across the axis.

question: A square paper is folded perfectly in half from left to right, and then exactly in half from top to bottom. Three parallel horizontal slits are cut side-by-side into the folded left edge of the resulting quarter. How will the paper appear when completely unfolded?
options: Six separate thin horizontal slits spread evenly across the paper
Three continuous horizontal slits crossing the entire width of the paper
A central square hole with three slits radiating outward
Three long continuous horizontal slits perfectly spanning the middle width of the paper
answer: Three long continuous horizontal slits perfectly spanning the middle width of the paper
explanation: Step 1: The paper is folded horizontally and vertically. The left edge of the final quarter is actually the primary vertical center fold of the original paper. Step 2: Cutting three horizontal slits into this vertical fold line means you are cutting perpendicularly right across the central axis. Step 3: Unfolding right to left mirrors all three slits horizontally, doubling their length. Unfolding bottom to top mirrors these three long slits vertically, duplicating the set. The final result is three continuous, elongated horizontal slits symmetrically spanning the central width.
trick: Slits cut perpendicularly into a main fold line double in length when opened. Since it's folded twice, these elongated slits then mirror vertically across the horizontal midline.
tip: Perpendicular slits on a double-folded center line mirror and double in length.
